transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop thinking about my hairline, you know? And the way my face looks. I work as a host at this lounge downtown, and the lighting there—it's this harsh, overhead pendant lighting that casts these terrible shadows. It makes me look so old and just... strange. I mean, the place itself is great, really upscale. We get a lot of local celebrities, actually. Just last week, that news anchor from channel 5 came in, and he ordered the seabass, which is funny because the seabass is usually our slowest seller on Tuesdays. I always tell the kitchen to prep less of it on Tuesdays, but they never listen. Anyway, my coworkers keep telling me they don't see what I'm talking about with my face, but I know it's there. I just can't stop obsessing over how bad I look under those lights.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, adjusting your hair, or avoiding certain lighting, because it helps you feel less anxious about your appearance?

Yeah, I... I do. Before my shift starts, I just get stuck in the bathroom. I keep checking the mirror over and over, and I'll take pictures on my phone from, like, a dozen different angles. I actually had to upgrade my phone recently because the camera on my old one was getting this weird blur to it. My daughter said it was just a smudge on the lens, but I don't think she knows what she's talking about. She's taking classes at the state college now—communications or something, which is ironic because she never texts me back. 

But anyway... I'm in there taking pictures, just constantly combing my hair forward to try and fix it, and I just keep replaying in my head exactly how the guests might see me when they walk up to the stand. I get so caught up in it that I end up being late, or I get too worked up to even go out front. And Gary, our floor manager, he hates that. He’s always on my case about being at the podium at exactly 4:45. Though honestly, Gary wears these awful clip-on ties, and I have no idea how he gets away with that in a place that serves eighty-dollar steaks, you know? It just brings down the whole vibe of the room. But yeah, I just... I can't stop checking.
Do you worry more about how you look to others, or about how people might react to you—like whether they’ll approve of you, reject you, or leave you?

Well, I guess... I'm not really sure if it's about them rejecting me, exactly. It's more just... I know they're looking at my hairline and the shadows on my face, and I can just feel them judging it. But honestly, people these days, they don't even look up from their phones half the time when they walk in. Just last night, this couple came in, dressed to the nines, and the guy didn't look up from his screen the entire time I was walking them to their table. And it's a long walk, too, all the way to the back patio. We just got these new patio heaters out there, the tall pyramid ones with the visible flame? They're supposed to be really high-end, but one of them keeps clicking and not lighting, and the maintenance guy, Sal, keeps saying he ordered the part. But Sal says he orders parts for everything and nothing ever gets fixed. Like the ice machine in the back hallway—it's been making this awful grinding noise since October. But anyway, I just... I don't know if I worry about them leaving me or anything like that. I just hate knowing how bad I look when I have to stand up there under those lights.
Do you believe that your hairline or the way your face looks under the lights is a flaw that others would notice and judge, even though they may not seem to react to it?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. I know they see it. Even if they don't say anything or just stare at their phones, I know it's there. Like I said when I first came in, I just can't stop thinking about my hairline and the way my face looks under those harsh pendant lights. It makes me look so old and strange, and it just consumes my thoughts. My coworkers keep telling me they don't see what I'm talking about, but they're just being nice, or maybe they don't want to deal with it. Speaking of dealing with things, one of the bartenders, Jessica, she's been trying to get her shifts covered for the last three weeks because she's auditioning for some local theater production. It's 'Our Town,' I think. Which is a classic, sure, but she keeps practicing her lines behind the bar, and it is just so distracting when I'm trying to seat people near the high-tops. And the high-tops are already a nightmare because the stools wobble. We put those little felt pads under them, but they just peel off after a day or two. The adhesive they use on those things is completely useless. But yeah, to answer your question, I definitely believe it's a flaw that everyone notices and judges me for, even if they pretend they don't.
Do you ever feel like the way your hairline and face look under the lights is something that others should see the way you do, even though they don’t seem to notice it?

Well, I don't know if they *should* see it the way I do, but... I mean, I just don't understand how they *don't*. It's right there. It's so obvious to me. But maybe they're just not paying attention, you know? People are so wrapped up in their own stuff. Like my neighbor, Dave. He just put up this massive privacy fence, right? Which is fine, but he completely blocked the sprinkler head on my side of the property line. I tried talking to him about it, but he just goes on and on about his landscaping vision. He's planting all these hydrangeas, which need a ton of water, so I don't know how he expects them to survive when he's messing with the irrigation. And the worst part is, the fence isn't even stained yet. It's just that raw, treated wood color that looks so cheap. I told my daughter about it, and she said I should just write him a note, but I don't want to be passive-aggressive. I prefer to just handle things directly, you know? But anyway... no, I don't necessarily think they *should* see it like I do, it's just frustrating that they act like it's not a big deal when it's all I can focus on.
Do these concerns about your appearance ever interfere with your ability to do your job or spend time with friends and family?

Yeah, it... it definitely gets in the way. I've actually been written up at work recently. I keep showing up late, or I just call out and miss shifts entirely because I just can't face those lights and the people looking at me. It takes me so long to try and fix my hair, to get the shadows right... and I've stopped doing a lot of things outside of work, too. Like, they do these staff photos, and I just won't go near them. And I used to go to gallery events, or go hiking with people, but I just... I can't handle being seen that way anymore. Especially hiking, you know? The sun is just brutal. It highlights every single flaw, every thin patch. And speaking of hiking, they just closed down the main trail at the state park near my house. Apparently, there was a mudslide after all that rain we got last week. Which is a shame, because it's the only trail with a decent incline. Now everyone is crowding onto the paved walking path around the lake, and it's just a mess. People walking four abreast, not paying attention, letting their dogs on those retractable leashes trip everybody up. I saw this one guy on a mountain bike nearly take out a whole family because he was going way too fast around a blind corner. You'd think they'd enforce the speed limit on those paths, but the park rangers are always just sitting in their trucks by the entrance kiosk. But yeah, I just... I don't go out much anymore. It's too hard.
Have you ever thought that there might be something wrong with your vision or perception, given that others don't seem to notice the flaws you see?

I mean, no. Not really. I know my eyes work fine. I just had my prescription checked, actually, because I thought maybe I needed bifocals. It turns out my distance vision is still 20/20, but I do need a little help with reading the menus at work. Which is so annoying, because the font they use for the wine list is ridiculous. It's this tiny, italicized script that looks like it belongs on a wedding invitation, not a bar menu. And they print it on this dark burgundy paper, so there's absolutely no contrast. I told the manager, Greg, that we need to reprint them, but he's so cheap. He won't spend a dime unless he has to. He's been driving the same beat-up Honda Civic since 2008, and the muffler is completely shot. You can hear him pull into the parking lot from three blocks away. It's embarrassing, honestly. But no, I don't think there's anything wrong with my perception. I just think people don't look closely enough. They just glance and move on. But when I look in the mirror, it's all right there.
Do these concerns about your appearance ever affect your relationships with friends or family, or cause you significant emotional distress even when you're not at work?

Well, yeah, like I was saying just a minute ago, it really does. The distress is... it's constant. That's exactly why I've stopped going to those gallery events with my friends, or going on those hikes. And like I said, it's why I'm getting written up at the restaurant for being late or missing my hosting shifts, and skipping the staff photos. I just can't handle my friends or my family seeing me like that. 

It causes huge fights, actually. My sister got really mad at me because I wouldn't go to her anniversary dinner last month. She had it catered by this local Italian place, which, honestly, is incredibly overrated. Their marinara sauce is way too sweet. I don't know why people insist on putting sugar in tomato sauce, it completely kills the natural acidity. If you just take the time to roast the garlic properly and use real San Marzano tomatoes, you don't need any sugar at all. I tried explaining that to her when she made baked ziti for Thanksgiving, but she gets so incredibly defensive about her cooking. She just bought this massive, expensive set of copper pots that she doesn't even know how to polish, so they're already turning green on the bottom. It's such a waste of money. If you aren't going to maintain copper, you should just stick to stainless steel, you know? 

But anyway... yeah, it definitely affects my relationships. I just can't be around them when I look like this, so I end up staying home, and they just don't get it.

When you're worried about how you look under the lights, is it mainly the appearance of your hairline and face that bothers you, or is it more about how you think others might judge or evaluate you as a person because of it?

Well, it's... it's really the appearance itself. That's why I'm here, honestly. I just can't stop thinking about my hairline and the way my face looks under those awful restaurant lights. It makes me look so old and... strange. And I know my coworkers tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, but they're just being polite, or they aren't looking close enough. It's the lights, mostly. They're these terrible exposed Edison bulbs. Greg, the manager, thinks they look "industrial chic," but they just cast these harsh, yellow shadows everywhere. It's like being in an interrogation room. And they give off so much heat, too. You stand near the host stand for ten minutes and you're sweating. I told Greg we should switch to LEDs. They make these really nice, warm-toned LED bulbs now that look exactly like incandescent, but they don't get hot and they use a fraction of the electricity. You'd think he'd be all over that, since he's so cheap about everything else, like those wine menus. I even found a bulk supplier online that sells them for like, two dollars a bulb. But he just brushed me off. He said he doesn't want to mess with the "ambiance." Ambiance! It's a mid-tier steakhouse, not a French bistro. We don't even have cloth napkins anymore, we switched to those thick paper ones that feel like sandpaper. But yeah... it's definitely how I look that bothers me, not what they think of me as a person. I just look so old under those lights.
Do you find yourself frequently comparing your appearance to others, or spending a lot of time thinking about how you look in photos or videos, even when you're not at work?

Well, yeah, it's... it's all I do, really. Especially before a shift. I mean, I'll stand in my bathroom at home for, I don't know, an hour? Just checking the mirror. I take pictures on my phone from all these different angles to see how the hairline looks, and then I try combing it forward, and then I take another picture. And I just keep replaying in my head how the guests are going to see me when they walk in the door. I get so worked up doing it that half the time I end up being late, or I just call out entirely because I can't face going out front. 

My bathroom mirror is actually terrible for it, though. It's one of those big, frameless builder-grade mirrors that came with the condo. The edges are starting to desilver, so there are these black spots creeping in along the bottom. I've been meaning to replace it, maybe get two separate oval mirrors with nice brushed nickel frames. I saw some at HomeGoods last week that were marked down on clearance because one had a tiny scratch on the back, but you couldn't even see it from the front. But then you have to deal with the drywall anchors, and if you don't hit a stud, it's a nightmare. My neighbor, Dave, tried to hang a heavy mirror in his hallway using those cheap plastic anchors, and the whole thing came crashing down in the middle of the night. Sounded like a bomb went off. He had glass everywhere for weeks, and it gouged the hardwood floors. He had to hire a guy to come in and sand the whole hallway down and restain it, but the stain doesn't quite match the living room now. You can totally see the line where they meet if the afternoon sun hits it right. 

But, uh, yeah, I do compare myself a lot. And taking the photos... it's just exhausting, trying to figure out how I'm going to look to everyone else before I even leave the house.

inference_history.note: The patient's preoccupation with their physical appearance, specifically their hairline and facial features under certain lighting, suggests Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). There is also a possible personality disorder with narcissistic traits (F60.5) given the context of their job as a lounge host and mention of local celebrities, though this is not yet confirmed.

These symptoms are consistent with body dysmorphic disorder (F45.22). They make these really nice, warm-toned LED bulbs now that look exactly like incandescent, but they don't get hot and they use a fraction of the electricity. You'd think he'd be all over that, since he's so cheap about everything else, like those wine menus. I even found a bulk supplier online that sells them for like, two dollars a bulb. But he just brushed me off. He said he doesn't want to mess with the "ambiance." Ambiance! It's a mid-tier steakhouse, not a French bistro. We don't even have cloth napkins anymore, we switched to those thick paper ones that feel like sandpaper. But yeah... it's definitely how I look that bothers me, not what they think of me as a person. I just look so old under those lights.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's concern about their appearance is part of a broader pattern of preoccupation with perceived physical defects that may indicate body dysmorphic disorder (BDD, F45.22) rather than a personality disorder (F60.5).
doctor.question: Do you find yourself frequently comparing your appearance to others, or spending a lot of time thinking about how you look in photos or videos, even when you're not at work?

target_item.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
target_item.manifestation: Before a shift I keep checking the bathroom mirror, taking phone pictures from different angles, combing my hair forward, and replaying how guests might see me until I’m late or too worked up to go out front.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repetitive mental acts (comparing appearance to others) and behaviors (spending a lot of time thinking about how you look in photos/videos), which directly relates to the patient's symptom of Appearance-Related Repetitive Behaviors.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it's... it's all I do, really. Especially before a shift. I mean, I'll stand in my bathroom at home for, I don't know, an hour? Just checking the mirror. I take pictures on my phone from all these different angles to see how the hairline looks, and then I try combing it forward, and then I take another picture. And I just keep replaying in my head how the guests are going to see me when they walk in the door. I get so worked up doing it that half the time I end up being late, or I just call out entirely because I can't face going out front. 

My bathroom mirror is actually terrible for it, though. It's one of those big, frameless builder-grade mirrors that came with the condo. The edges are starting to desilver, so there are these black spots creeping in along the bottom. I've been meaning to replace it, maybe get two separate oval mirrors with nice brushed nickel frames. I saw some at HomeGoods last week that were marked down on clearance because one had a tiny scratch on the back, but you couldn't even see it from the front. But then you have to deal with the drywall anchors, and if you don't hit a stud, it's a nightmare. My neighbor, Dave, tried to hang a heavy mirror in his hallway using those cheap plastic anchors, and the whole thing came crashing down in the middle of the night. Sounded like a bomb went off. He had glass everywhere for weeks, and it gouged the hardwood floors. He had to hire a guy to come in and sand the whole hallway down and restain it, but the stain doesn't quite match the living room now. You can totally see the line where they meet if the afternoon sun hits it right. 

But, uh, yeah, I do compare myself a lot. And taking the photos... it's just exhausting, trying to figure out how I'm going to look to everyone else before I even leave the house.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance (hairline and facial shadows under lighting), repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, photo taking), and significant distress and impairment in occupational and social functioning. These symptoms align with body dysmorphic disorder rather than a personality disorder, as the focus is on a specific perceived physical defect rather than pervasive maladaptive personality traits.
